# Corridor Planning Study: Albany, NY to Buffalo, NY Intercity Passenger Rail

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This study evaluates three conceptual passenger rail alternatives connecting Albany, NY and Buffalo, NY based on 5000 simulation runs per route. Alternative 1, the Existing corridor upgrade, spans 284 miles entirely within existing rail corridors (100.0%) with 4 stations, presenting the lowest median (P50) capital cost at $6.9B and the shortest median (P50) schedule of 13.6 years. Alternative 2, the New direct alignment, covers 275 miles with 2 stations, requiring 229 miles of new track length, a median (P50) cost of $13.0B, and a median (P50) delivery timeline of 14.8 years.

Alternative 3, designated Via intermediate cities, extends 315 miles to serve 5 stations, utilizing 152 miles of new track and a 51.7% share on existing rail corridors. This alternative serves the highest counts for residents near stations (1.35 million) and residents near alignment (3.32 million), with a median (P50) cost of $13.2B and a median (P50) time to opening of 14.7 years. Population metrics are not passenger ridership forecasts, and presence on existing corridors does not confirm track access or operating rights.

## Corridor Description

The Albany, NY to Buffalo, NY corridor connects upstate New York population centers across varying physical profiles. Alternative 1 (Existing corridor upgrade) follows existing rights-of-way for 284 miles with 0 miles of new track, calling at Albany, Utica, Syracuse, and Buffalo. It encompasses 3.12 million residents within 10 miles of the line, 965 thousand residents within 10 km of stations, 15 environmental flag entries, and 8 river crossings. Alternative 2 (New direct alignment) is a greenfield-focused route of 275 miles with 16.6% share on existing corridors and 229 miles of new track, serving Albany and Buffalo directly. It includes 2.77 million residents near the alignment, 603 thousand residents near stations, 3 environmental flag entries, and 2 river crossings.

Alternative 3 (Via intermediate cities) covers 315 miles through Albany, Utica, Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo, balancing greenfield segments with a 51.7% share on existing rail corridors and 152 miles of new track. It records 3.32 million residents near the alignment, 1.35 million residents near its 5 stations, 7 environmental flag entries, and 5 river crossings. Share on existing rail corridors indicates shared path alignments only and does not establish ownership access, spare capacity, or operating permission.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Reported figures are illustrative estimates derived from 5000 Monte Carlo runs and do not constitute engineering budgets. For Alternative 1, capital cost ranges from a low (P10) of $5.6B to a median (P50) of $6.9B and a high (P90) of $8.6B, with delivery times estimated at a low (P10) of 11.7 years, median (P50) of 13.6 years, and high (P90) of 15.7 years. 

Alternative 2 requires higher capital commitment, exhibiting a low (P10) cost of $10.8B, a median (P50) of $13.0B, and a high (P90) of $15.7B. Projected timelines for Alternative 2 span a low (P10) of 13.1 years, a median (P50) of 14.8 years, and a high (P90) of 16.8 years. For Alternative 3, the capital cost spans a low (P10) of $11.0B, a median (P50) of $13.2B, and a high (P90) of $15.9B, paired with delivery schedules between a low (P10) of 12.9 years, median (P50) of 14.7 years, and high (P90) of 16.6 years.

## Funding Strategy

Federal grant and credit programs provide pathways to assemble capital for each alternative. All alternatives demonstrate high alignment with the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID), offering an initial $500K for Step 1 scoping to feed the federal capital pipeline. For primary construction, the FRA Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National) program offers grant funding up to $3.0B per award, representing 43.6% of median (P50) cost for Alternative 1, 23.1% for Alternative 2, and 22.8% for Alternative 3. Because the median (P50) costs of all options exceed the single award ceiling, implementation would require phased awards.

Supplemental grant sources include Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI), which caps near $250M per award and could fund discrete packages such as sidings or grade separations (covering 3.6% of median cost for Alternative 1 and 1.9% for Alternatives 2 and 3). USDOT BUILD grants provide up to $25M per award for station or crossing elements, covering 0.4% of median costs for Alternative 1 and 0.2% for Alternatives 2 and 3. To meet non-federal match requirements, Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing (RRIF) loans from the USDOT Build America Bureau could finance non-federal shares: $1.4B for Alternative 1, and $2.6B each for Alternatives 2 and 3, subject to identified repayment revenue.

## Risks

Project delivery and operational readiness face several key unmodeled conditions and corridor-specific constraints:
- Railroad Coordination and Capacity: Track capacity, freight conflicts, train paths, and access agreements with host railroads were not modeled; high existing corridor reuse (100.0% in Alternative 1, 51.7% in Alternative 3) does not guarantee operating permissions.
- Operations and Economics: Service frequency, timetable, span of service, operating and maintenance costs, fare revenue, and annual operating subsidy were not evaluated.
- Demand and Service Quality: Ridership or station-pair demand forecasts, door-to-door or in-train travel times, travel-time competitiveness with driving, bus or air, and on-time performance and reliability were not modeled.
- Physical and Fleet Requirements: Rolling stock, maintenance facilities, electrification costs, benefit-cost ratio, emissions, and safety outcomes were omitted from the analysis.
- Environmental and Waterway Crossings: Construction involves physical risks, including 15 environmental flag entries and 8 river crossings for Alternative 1, 3 environmental flag entries and 2 river crossings for Alternative 2, and 7 environmental flag entries and 5 river crossings for Alternative 3.

## Next Steps

To advance the corridor, planning bodies should focus on addressing unmodeled technical areas and formalizing federal entry points:
- Apply for the FRA Corridor Identification and Development Program to secure $500K in Step 1 scoping support and enter the project pipeline.
- Initiate formal discussions with host railroad entities to evaluate track capacity, freight conflicts, train paths, and framework access agreements.
- Conduct ridership and station-pair demand forecasting alongside door-to-door and in-train travel time analyses across competing highway and air modes.
- Model service frequencies, timetable options, span of service, and expected on-time performance and reliability.
- Develop operations and maintenance cost models, fare revenue projections, and required annual operating subsidy estimates.
- Detail rolling stock technology, maintenance facility sites, electrification feasibility, and full benefit-cost ratio analyses.
- Perform field-level environmental reviews for corridor footprints, addressing river crossings and flagged environmental areas.
